title: Follow-Up Report, Alpha School Speaks
author: Benjamin Riley
summary: Riley follows up his reporting on Alpha School's high school boot camp after the school responded, not by rebutting him, but by promoting a microsite that he reads as confirming his account in full. He walks through the site's grid of eighteen required life skills, which includes watching a full season of Survivor for critical thinking, building a Twitter account to 100 followers, and a physically demanding Dirty Job, and he notes that the school gave three of these extended written defenses that an AI detector scored as majority machine generated. The core of his critique is epistemological: Alpha School treats a measurable Key Performance Indicator as the only trustworthy evidence of learning, and its own explanations say so, disparaging teacher judgment as subjective uncertainty. Riley also flags the timing problem, since Alpha School's publicist called his screenshots mischaracterizations while never pointing him to the microsite that described the same activities. He records two student reactions, one of whom deleted a joking post after being told to. His sharpest practical objection is to the SAT requirement, a 200-point jump inside eight weeks, which he considers close to impossible without cooking the books. The piece ends by addressing Alpha students directly with an argument for agency, reading and character over metrics.
points: The microsite's own text makes the case against subjective teacher judgment explicitly, treating an objective metric as the only way a student can know they succeeded.
Riley ran the three extended activity defenses through Pangram, which scored them 61 to 73 percent AI generated, and he is careful to say he is not endorsing AI detection in classrooms.
Alpha School's publicist described his source screenshots as mischaracterizations while never directing him to the public microsite describing the same boot camp tasks.
The SAT requirement of a 200-point gain in eight weeks is singled out as the least funny item, because meeting it honestly would be nearly impossible given the program's academic thinness.
The boot camp is framed by the school as bringing students to a shared starting line, but Riley notes students remain in it until every objective is hit, with no stated cap on duration.
quotes: The main event is this: Yesterday, Alpha School indirectly confirmed the entirety of my reporting, and promoted a microsite for its bootcamp.
Notably, however, if this site was live prior to my story being published, Alpha School never pointed me to it, despite my repeated requests for comment.
The new microsite lists 18 specific “life skills” that students must complete as “prerequisites for the deeper, more advanced work ahead
I analyzed each deep dive using Pangram, which scored them as 61% to 73% AI-generated (for more on this, see footnote).
We do not believe that shielding students from a powerful technology that is essential to success in a modern world is a better choice than preparing students to use it well.
If mastery depends on a teacher’s judgment, a student can always wonder whether they truly succeeded. However, an objective metric removes that uncertainty.

it’s become clear that for Alpha School, truth and value do not exist absent a Key Performance Indicator. The problem is that not all of life revolves around KPIs (unless they get their way!), so you end up having to concoct the absurd sorts of measures we see here
Slightly less funny, though, are the core academic performance requirements, and in particular the SAT scores, the very first “life skill” listed.
